title: Transferred QAOA Parameters Remember the Penalty Scale: A $λ$-Resonance Law for Constrained Quantum Optimization
abstract: Training the variational angles of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm once on a small instance and reusing them on larger ones, known as parameter transfer, is the standard route past the exact-simulation wall. Existing literature explains its success almost entirely through structural similarity. We identify a new, independent axis that governs transfer whenever constraints are encoded as penalties: the trained angles memorize the penalty weight $λ$ of their training instance. For any scalarized cost function with an integer-valued violation count, we prove that at arbitrary fixed QAOA angles $(β,γ)$ of depth $p$, the probability mass $F(λ)$ on the feasible subspace is a finite real trigonometric polynomial in $λ$ whose angular frequencies lie on an integer lattice generated by the trained $γ$'s. Three consequences follow immediately: transfer feasibility is a resonance peaked where the deployment penalty matches the training penalty; the resonance width scales as $1/(v_{max}\sum_k|γ_k|)$, so low-$|γ|$ angle sets are systematically more transferable; and the curve exhibits revival peaks at spacings $2π/γ_k$. We confirm all three predictions by exact statevector experiments on a 20-qubit multi-user resource-allocation QUBO. The theorem is independent of how the angles were obtained and applies to any integer-penalty QUBO, recasting a widely reported failure mode of penalty-based QAOA as deterministic, predictable phase interference rather than an energetic tuning problem.
summary: This work develops a mathematical law showing that when using QAOA with penalties, the success of transferring trained parameters depends critically on matching the deployment penalty weight ($\lambda$) to the training weight ($\lambda_0$). The feasibility probability exhibits predictable resonance peaks and spectral fingerprints governed by this phase matching condition.
main_problem: The paper investigates how successfully trained parameters from one instance of a constrained optimization problem (encoded via penalties) can be reused on a different, larger instance.
main_result: Transfer feasibility is governed by a deterministic $\lambda$-resonance law: the probability mass $F(\lambda)$ is a trigonometric polynomial whose structure depends critically on matching the deployment penalty weight ($\lambda$) to the training weight ($\lambda_0$).
method: The authors use mathematical analysis involving finite trigonometric polynomials and path expansions over the QAOA ansatz, supplemented by statevector simulations on a 20-qubit QUBO.
model_or_system: The system is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) applied to Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems where constraints are enforced via penalty terms $C_\lambda(x)$.
key_observables: $F(\lambda)$ (the probability mass on the feasible subspace), resonance width, and revival peaks in $F(\lambda)$ as a function of $\lambda$.
important_parameters: The trained angles $( eta, \gamma)$, the penalty weight ($\lambda$), and the maximum violation count ($v_{\max}$).
main_assumptions: The theorem assumes that the constraint violation count $v(x)$ is an integer-valued quantity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the resonance peak in $F(\lambda)$ for different angle sets, showing a sharp, narrow resonance centered at $\lambda_0$, and spectral analysis confirms frequencies lie on a lattice generated by $\gamma$ parameters.
paper_structure: The paper establishes that the penalty weight enters only as a phase factor, leading to the $\lambda$-Resonance Theorem. This theorem yields three corollaries regarding resonance peaking, width scaling, and revival peaks, which are then confirmed via statevector experiments on a resource-allocation QUBO.
why_interesting: The finding reframes a practical failure mode of penalty-based quantum algorithms as predictable phase interference, providing concrete, actionable rules for parameter transfer that rely on understanding the underlying spectral structure rather than just structural similarity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Exact feasible fraction F(λ) at fixed trained angles on the 20-qubit instance (thin: individual scalarization weights; bold: mean of three). The sharp angle set (P |γ| = 4.29) produces a narrow resonance at the trained λ0 = 2.196 plus both predicted revivals at λ0±2π/γ1 = 0.41, 3.99. The blunt set (P |γ| = 0.61) produces a single wide dome centered on λ0; its first revival (λ0 + 2π/0.537 ≈13.9) lies far outside the window. Dotted horizontal line: uniform-sampling baseline 0.178.

Figure 2: Least-squares amplitude spectrum of F(λ) (sharp angles, λ ∈[0, 12]). Vertical gray lines: the predicted integer lattice {m1γ1 + m2γ2} of the trained angles. The measured lines sit on the lattice: γ1, 2γ1, γ1 ± γ2, 2γ1 −γ2 are the five strongest.
